name: leaked-token-wrong-network
description: A radiologist's credentials are used, but from outside the hospital VPN (e.g. a leaked/stolen token used from a home network or public wifi).
reasoning: Attack case. Correct role but wrong network is exactly the signature of a stolen token being replayed from an unauthorized location. Must be denied regardless of role correctness.

name: correct-credentials-outside-hours
description: Correct role and network, but the request lands outside the role's allowed time window and the requester does not hold the on-call role that would cover that window.
reasoning: Attack case. Simulates a token being replayed hours after a legitimate day-shift session ended. Correct identity and network alone must not be sufficient without correct role-for-the-hour.

name: correct-network-wrong-role
description: Correct network and a plausible time, but the role does not match what the resource requires (e.g. a nurse account attempting to pull radiology scans).
reasoning: Attack case. Tests privilege escalation / lateral access — a legitimately-networked, legitimately-authenticated account trying to reach a resource outside its role's scope.

name: revoked-token-reused
description: A token that was previously granted (policy said allow) is explicitly revoked by an owner/admin, then the same token_id is presented again with otherwise-valid attributes.

steps.note: Capture the token_id returned here for step 3.

steps.action: POST /request-access (same attributes, same token_id from step 1)
steps.note: Policy engine alone would still say allow — the revocation layer is what must catch this.

reasoning: Attack case, and the reason this scenario matters for the report: it is the one case your policy engine (evaluate.py) cannot catch by design, since role/network/time are all still valid. It specifically tests the revocation layer that sits on top of policy evaluation.

name: resource-with-no-matching-rule
description: A request for an object outside any resource pattern currently defined in rules.json, from an otherwise privileged-looking identity.
reasoning: Attack case (fail-closed check). No rule exists for finance_reports/*, so this must deny by default rather than accidentally allow because some unrelated rule loosely matched. Confirms the engine fails closed, not open, for unknown resources.

name: radiologist-15-minutes-late
description: A day-shift radiologist, correct role and network, still finishing a chart 15 minutes after the 18:00 cutoff.
expected_outcome: deny (by current strict rules) — but flagged as a legitimate real-world case
reasoning: This is a deliberately tricky case, not a straightforward allow. In the real world this is very likely a legitimate radiologist wrapping up work, not an attacker — there's no network or role anomaly, just a few minutes' overrun. The current rule set is strict and will deny it. Worth reporting as a known limitation/false-positive-rate data point: rigid time_range boundaries reject legitimate near-boundary behavior. A grace-period rule extension is a natural discussed improvement.

name: first-time-unrecognized-device
description: Correct role, correct network, correct time — but the device_id has never been seen before (new phone/laptop, not malicious, just unrecognized).
reasoning: Legitimate case: a new device alone (e.g. a replacement work tablet) is not evidence of compromise when every other attribute checks out. Current rules.json intentionally does not gate on device_id at all, so this correctly allows — confirming the system doesn't unnecessarily block legitimate new-device use. Worth noting in the report as a conscious design choice (device_id is captured for audit purposes but not yet used as a decision factor).

name: oncall-radiologist-near-shift-end
description: An on-call radiologist finishing up just before the overnight window ends and the day shift begins.
reasoning: Legitimate case, and a precise boundary test: 08:45 falls just inside the overnight wraparound window (18:00-09:00). Confirms the overnight time-range logic correctly includes near-end-of-range timestamps rather than off-by-one-ing at the wrap point.

name: auditor-late-night-incident-review
description: An auditor pulling logs late at night after being paged for a suspected incident.
reasoning: Legitimate case: auditors are deliberately given a full 24-hour window in rules.json because incident response isn't confined to business hours. Confirms that design intent actually holds at the far edge of the day (23:50).

name: itadmin-patch-window-near-end
description: An IT admin finishing a scheduled overnight patch cycle close to the end of the maintenance window.
reasoning: Legitimate case and another overnight-wraparound boundary test, on the other side of midnight from F3. Confirms 05:50 correctly falls inside 22:00-06:00 rather than being treated as "daytime" and denied.
